seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 67 HTS Chapter 88 lines: airplanes, helicopters, gliders, spacecraft, parachutes, flight simulators, drones and aircraft parts. Almost all Free at base; when civil aircraft (general note 6) are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties; the Section 232 drone duty of 25% to 100%; China's 25% List 1 duty.
keywords: Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft

overview.intro:
Chapter 88 covers aircraft and spacecraft: balloons, gliders and hang gliders (8801), helicopters, airplanes, satellites and launch vehicles (8802), parachutes and paragliders (8804), launching gear and ground flight simulators (8805), unmanned aircraft (drones, 8806) and parts of aircraft and drones (8807). **66 of the 67 tariff lines are Free** under the general rate; only parachutes (8804) pay a base duty of 3%. The U.S. imported **$33.85B** of Chapter 88 goods in 2025, mostly airplanes, helicopters and aircraft parts from Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Brazil and Japan.

What decides the duty today is **civil-aircraft status** and origin. Civil aircraft, engines, parts and ground flight simulators that meet the criteria of **general note 6** (the Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft: used in aircraft and covered by an FAA certificate or an FAA-recognized foreign airworthiness approval, not bought for the Department of Defense or Coast Guard unless certified) are exempt from the **2026 Section 301 duties** of 10% or 12.5% (U.S. note 52(d), 9903.05.88) and from **Brazil's 25%** (note 50(a)(iv), 9903.05.05). So a certified civil airliner, helicopter or part enters **Free** from the EU, the UK, Japan, Brazil and most other countries. Articles that do not qualify (military aircraft and parts, and spacecraft and satellite parts, which are not on the civil-aircraft list) pay the Section 301 duty for their origin. **China** pays 25% under Section 301 List 1 on helicopters, airplanes, drones and parts (7.5% on balloons and gliders under List 4A), with no civil-aircraft exception. **Drones** of 8806 also pay the Section 232 duty that began September 3, 2026: +100% with thermal imaging or over 25 kg, +25% for other drones up to 25 kg (9903.08.21 / 9903.08.22). The 2019 Airbus-dispute duties on EU and UK aircraft (9903.89.05) have been suspended since 2021, and Proclamation 11040 (July 9, 2026) found aircraft imports a national-security threat but imposed **no tariff** for now.

productGroups.label: Balloons and dirigibles; gliders, hang gliders and other non-powered aircraft
productGroups.blurb: Balloons, airships, gliders and hang gliders: 3 lines, all Free. Non-powered aircraft that meet general note 6 are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties; China pays 7.5% (List 4A).

productGroups.label: Other aircraft (for example, helicopters, airplanes, except unmanned aircraft of heading 8806); spacecraft (including satellites) and suborbital and spacecraft launch vehicles
productGroups.blurb: Helicopters, airplanes by unladen weight, satellites and launch vehicles: 36 lines, all Free, with separate statistical lines for military and civil, new and used aircraft. Certified civil aircraft are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties; spacecraft (8802.60) are not on that list.

productGroups.label: Parachutes (including dirigible parachutes and paragliders) and rotochutes; parts thereof and accessories thereto
productGroups.blurb: Parachutes, paragliders, rotochutes and their parts: 1 line, 3% (Free under USMCA and most FTAs). Not on the civil-aircraft list, so the 2026 Section 301 duty applies to it.

productGroups.label: Aircraft launching gear; deck-arrestor or similar gear; ground flying trainers; parts of the foregoing articles
productGroups.blurb: Aircraft launching gear, deck arrestors, air combat simulators and other ground flight simulators and their parts: 3 lines, all Free. Only flight simulators of 8805.29 are on the civil-aircraft exemption list.

productGroups.label: Unmanned aircraft
productGroups.blurb: Unmanned aircraft by take-off weight, remote-controlled or not, and passenger drones: 11 lines, all Free at base. Since September 3, 2026 drones of 8806.21–8806.99 pay a Section 232 duty of 25% or 100% on top of other duties.

productGroups.label: Parts of goods of heading 8801, 8802 or 8806
productGroups.blurb: Propellers and rotors, undercarriages, other parts of airplanes, helicopters and drones, and parts of communications satellites: 13 lines, all Free, with statistical lines for civil-aircraft use. The biggest import line of the chapter.

workedExamples.title: A new airliner from France
workedExamples.body: Passenger airplanes over 15,000 kg are **Free** under the general rate. France pays the EU's 2026 Section 301 duty of **10% in place of the base rate** (9903.05.39), but civil aircraft that meet general note 6 are exempt (U.S. note 52(d), heading 9903.05.88). A certified civil airliner therefore pays **$0**. The 15% large-civil-aircraft duty of 2020 (9903.89.05) has been suspended for EU products since 2021. A military transport (statistical suffix .20 or .30) cannot use the civil-aircraft exemption and pays 10%: **$10M on a $100M aircraft**.

workedExamples.title: A regional jet from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Multiple-engine airplanes of 2,000–4,536 kg (and 8802.40 for heavier jets) are Free at base. Brazil pays **25%** (9903.05.01) plus the **12.5%** 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.27), 37.5% in all. A civil aircraft that meets general note 6 is exempt from both (notes 50(a)(iv) and 52(d), headings 9903.05.05 and 9903.05.88), so it pays **$0**. Without the civil-aircraft certification it would pay $375,000 on $1M.

workedExamples.title: Aircraft parts from Japan and China
workedExamples.body: Other parts of airplanes and helicopters for civil aircraft are Free. From **Japan** the 2026 Section 301 duty is **12.5% in place of the base rate** (9903.05.49), lifted for general-note-6 civil aircraft parts (9903.05.88): **$0**. From **China** the same part pays the **25%** List 1 duty (9903.88.01) even when it is a certified civil aircraft part, because note 20 has no civil-aircraft exception; only the 12.5% (9903.05.31) is lifted. On $10,000 that is **$2,500**, or $3,750 for a non-civil part.

workedExamples.title: A small camera drone from China or Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Remote-controlled drones of 250 g to 7 kg are Free at base. Since September 3, 2026 a drone without thermal imaging pays the **25%** Section 232 duty (9903.08.22) and one with thermal imaging **100%** (9903.08.21). From **China** add 12.5% (9903.05.31) and 25% List 1 (9903.88.01): **62.5%** without thermal imaging ($625 on a $1,000 drone) or **137.5%** with it. From **Vietnam**: 12.5% + 25% = **37.5%**, or 112.5% with thermal imaging. Drones on the Blue UAS lists or the FCC Conditional Approval list on September 2, 2026 start paying the drone duty on February 9, 2027.

workedExamples.title: A drone from Germany or the UK with allied critical components
workedExamples.body: If the importer certifies that substantially all the drone's critical components and technology come from the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, the EU or the UK (U.S. note 43(d)), an EU drone's Section 232 duty becomes **15% in all** (9903.08.24) and a UK drone's **+10%** (9903.08.23). The 2026 Section 301 duty still applies on top: the calculator gives **25%** for Germany (10% + 15%) and **20%** for the UK (10% + 10%); a drone that meets general note 6 drops the Section 301 part.

workedExamples.title: Parachutes from Canada
workedExamples.body: Parachutes pay **3%**, the only base duty in the chapter. With a USMCA claim a Canadian parachute is **Free**, and note 52(g) (9903.05.93) also lifts the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada. Without the claim it pays 3% + 10% = **13%**. Parachutes are not on the civil-aircraft list, so general note 6 does not help.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** For the purposes of this chapter, the expression "unmanned aircraft" means any aircraft, other than those of heading 8801, designed to be flown without a pilot on board. They may be designed to carry a payload or equipped with permanently integrated digital cameras or other equipment which would enable them to perform utilitarian functions during their flight. The expression "unmanned aircraft", however, does not cover flying toys, designed solely for amusement purposes (heading 9503).

**Subheading note 1.** For the purposes of subheadings 8802.11 to 8802.40, the expression "unladen weight" means the weight of the machine in normal flying order, excluding the weight of the crew and of fuel and equipment other than permanently fitted items of equipment.

seo.title: Aircraft & Drone Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Civil Aircraft Exemption, Section 232 Drones, Airbus Duties (HTS Ch. 88) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for aircraft, drone and aircraft-parts imports since 2025: the civil-aircraft exemptions in the 2025 UK, EU, Japan and Korea deals, the end of the IEEPA duties and Section 122, the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties and their civil-aircraft exemption, the Section 232 drone duty, the Section 232 aircraft finding with no tariff, and the suspended Airbus-dispute duties.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). The base rates did not change: 66 of the 67 Chapter 88 lines are Free in both, and parachutes stay at 3%.

The extra duties changed a lot, and civil aircraft were treated differently from almost everything else. In 2025 aircraft paid the IEEPA duties: 25% (later 35%) on non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico and the reciprocal tariff on most other countries. Civil aircraft and parts were then exempted country by country as trade deals were implemented: the **UK** from June 30, 2025, the **EU** from September 1, **Japan** from September 16 and **South Korea**, **Switzerland** and **Liechtenstein** from November 14, 2025; Brazil's 40% IEEPA duty excepted them from the start. All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them (civil aircraft exempt, 9903.03.05) expired on **July 23, 2026**.

Today the **2026 Section 301 duties** on 60 economies (from July 24, 2026) and **Brazil's 25%** (from July 22, 2026) reach every line, with an exemption for general-note-6 civil aircraft; China pays its **2018–2019 Section 301** duties; and **drones** pay the **Section 232 drone duty** from September 3, 2026. **Proclamation 11040** (July 9, 2026) found that imports of commercial aircraft, jet engines and parts threaten national security but imposed no tariff, directing negotiations with an update due within 180 days. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 88 goods.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 88 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies and their civil-aircraft exemption (note 52(d)), Brazil Section 301 (note 50), China Section 301 Lists 1, 3 and 4A (note 20), the Section 232 drone duty (note 43), Russia's column 2 and 35% rates (note 30) and the 200% Russian aluminum duty on one parts line (note 19), the pending Nicaragua duty (note 29), and the suspended large-civil-aircraft duties on EU and UK products (note 21). Also the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the Section 232 aircraft action (Proclamation 11040, no tariff), the Canada Section 338 duties (which list no Chapter 88 line) and the 2017–2018 large civil aircraft AD/CVD case (no order). For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 88 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 67 Chapter 88 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered. 66 lines are Free; parachutes (8804) are 3%.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. The 25% List 1 duty on Chinese helicopters, airplanes, drones and aircraft parts continues.

changes.title: Section 232 drone duty takes effect
changes.detail: Proclamation 11055 (August 13, 2026) imposed Section 232 duties on unmanned aircraft systems and components (U.S. note 43). In Chapter 88: +100% on drones over 25 kg (8806.24, .29, .94, .99) and on drones up to 25 kg with thermal imaging (9903.08.21), +25% on drones up to 25 kg without thermal imaging (9903.08.22), and +100% on parts of 8807 only for drone systems over 25 kg (not retail-delivery, agricultural or Department of War). Products of the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and Liechtenstein pay 15% in all, and the UK +10%, with a critical-components certification (9903.08.23 / .24). Approved onshoring plans import duty-free (9903.08.25 / .26).

changes.title: Drone duty for Blue UAS and FCC Conditional Approval products from February 9, 2027
changes.detail: For companies and products on the Department of War's Blue UAS Cleared List or Blue UAS Framework, or the FCC's Conditional Approval list, on September 2, 2026, and their components, the Section 232 drone duty starts 180 days after the proclamation: February 9, 2027 (Proclamation 11055 clause 7).

changes.title: FCC proposes to bar imports of certain foreign military-grade drones
changes.detail: The FCC's Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau and Office of Engineering and Technology sought comment (due September 2, 2026) on prohibiting the continued importation and marketing of certain military-grade foreign-made drones and drone critical components on the FCC Covered List, under 47 CFR 2.939. No final action had been published by October 13, 2026. The Covered List already bars new FCC equipment authorizations for drones and drone critical components produced in a foreign country (47 CFR 2.903; 91 FR 57798).

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies; civil aircraft exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect, reaching all 67 Chapter 88 lines. Civil aircraft, engines, parts and ground flight simulators that meet general note 6 are exempt on the 60 lines of the listed provisions (U.S. note 52(d), 9903.05.88), whether or not "Free (C)" is claimed. Spacecraft, parachutes, launching gear, air combat simulators and satellite parts are not on that list. Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA are exempt (notes 52(g)–(h)).

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301: 25%, civil aircraft exempt
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Civil aircraft that meet general note 6 are exempt on the same provisions as note 52(d) (note 50(a)(iv), 9903.05.05), which covers Embraer aircraft and parts. Other Chapter 88 goods of Brazil pay 25% plus the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty.

changes.title: Section 232 aircraft: negotiations, update due by January 5, 2027
changes.detail: Proclamation 11040 directs the Secretary of Commerce and the Trade Representative to negotiate agreements on imports of commercial aircraft, jet engines and parts and to update the President within 180 days (by January 5, 2027). The President may consider other remedies, including tariffs, if no agreement is reached or it is not carried out (19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A)).

changes.title: Section 232 aircraft finding: no tariff imposed
changes.detail: Commerce found that imports of commercial aircraft, jet engines and their parts threaten to impair national security and recommended negotiations and no immediate tariffs. Proclamation 11040 concurred and imposed no duty, so certified civil aircraft and parts still enter at the rates above. Chapter 99 has no heading for this action.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still exempt Canadian and Mexican goods from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; civil aircraft exempt
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Civil aircraft, engines, parts and simulators that met general note 6 were exempt on the listed provisions (9903.03.05), and USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08). Drones and other non-certified articles paid 10%.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 88 line. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: South Korea, Switzerland and Liechtenstein: civil aircraft exempted from the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Implementing the U.S.-Korea deal and the U.S.-Switzerland-Liechtenstein framework, Commerce exempted civil aircraft (other than military and unmanned aircraft), engines, parts and simulators meeting general note 6 from the countries' reciprocal tariffs (headings 9903.02.81, 9903.02.85, 9903.02.90), effective for goods entered from November 14, 2025. Ended with all IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Japan: civil aircraft exempted from the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14345 and Commerce's notice exempted Japanese products under the Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft, except unmanned aircraft, from the 15% reciprocal tariff (9903.96.02). Ended with all IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: EU: civil aircraft and parts exempted from the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Under Executive Order 14346 and the U.S.-EU framework, Commerce exempted EU civil aircraft, engines, parts and simulators meeting general note 6 from the 15% reciprocal tariff (heading 9903.02.76), retroactive to goods entered from September 1, 2025 (notice published September 25). Ended with all IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil: 40% IEEPA duty; civil aircraft excepted

Civil aircraft, engines, parts and simulators meeting general note 6 were excepted (9903.01.82, U.S. note 2(x)(iv)), so certified Embraer aircraft and parts paid only the 10% reciprocal tariff. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 investigation of drones begins
changes.detail: Commerce initiated a Section 232 investigation of imports of unmanned aircraft systems and their parts and components (comments due August 6, 2025). It led to Proclamation 11055.

changes.title: UK: civil aircraft exempted from the 10% reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14309 implemented the U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal; from June 30, 2025 UK civil aircraft (all aircraft other than military aircraft), engines, parts and simulators meeting general note 6 were exempt from the 10% reciprocal tariff (9903.96.01, U.S. note 35(a)). changes.title: Section 232 investigation of commercial aircraft and jet engines begins
changes.detail: Commerce initiated a Section 232 investigation of imports of commercial aircraft, jet engines and their parts (comments due June 3, 2025). It concluded with Proclamation 11040 (no tariff).

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff covers aircraft and parts
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico from April 5, 2025, later country-specific rates. changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 88 goods were **$33.85B in 2025**, down 5.7% from $35.91B in 2024, the highest year in the series, and up from $28.60B in 2020. Two product groups make up almost all of it: **parts** of aircraft and drones (8807, $17.55B), of which other parts of airplanes and helicopters (8807.30) alone were $14.65B, and **complete aircraft** (8802, $15.49B), mainly airplanes over 15,000 kg ($9.58B, down from $12.52B) and 2,000–15,000 kg ($4.77B).

**Canada** ($9.10B, 27%) ships both complete aircraft ($6.34B) and parts ($2.26B). **France** ($6.14B) is mostly complete aircraft ($4.20B), as are **Germany** ($2.75B, down from $5.51B in 2024) and **Brazil** ($2.42B, $2.19B of aircraft). The **United Kingdom** ($2.48B), **Japan** ($2.11B) and **Mexico** ($1.70B) ship almost only parts.

**Drones** (8806) were $190.5M in 2025, down from $480.5M in 2024; small remote-controlled drones of 250 g to 7 kg (8806.22) fell from $219.0M to $84.5M. Vietnam ($42.4M) and China ($29.9M) were the largest drone suppliers.

2025 is the latest full year of trade data, so the 2026 Section 301 and Section 232 drone duties are not yet visible in these figures. UN Comtrade does not say which imports were certified civil aircraft articles, the status that decides whether the 2026 Section 301 duties apply. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Almost every Chapter 88 line is Free at base, so the totals are the extra duties.

Cells show two totals where it matters: **civil aircraft** (the article meets general note 6, the Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft, SPI "C": it is used in aircraft and covered by an FAA certificate or an FAA-recognized foreign approval, so the 2026 Section 301 duty is lifted by 9903.05.88 and Brazil's 25% by 9903.05.05) and **not civil aircraft** (military articles, uncertified goods, or no claim). A total with no label in a cell with labelled totals belongs to lines that are not on the civil-aircraft list, so the answer does not change their duty. Spacecraft, parachutes, launching gear, air combat simulators and satellite parts are not on the civil-aircraft list and always pay the Section 301 duty for their origin. China's 25% List 1 duty has no civil-aircraft exception. **Drones** (8806) show a range: +25% (no thermal imaging) or +100% (thermal imaging, or over 25 kg) under Section 232, on top of the country's duties; passenger drones (8806.10) are outside the drone duty. The lower partner rates for drones (15% in all for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland; +10% for the UK) need a critical-components certification and are not shown.

seo.title: Importing Aircraft, Drones & Aircraft Parts: Civil Aircraft Certification, FAA Rules & Duty Savings (HTS Ch. 88) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Tariff engineering for HTS Chapter 88: claim the general note 6 civil-aircraft exemption (19 CFR 10.183), use USMCA, the drone partner and onshoring rates, repairs-abroad and returned-goods provisions, temporary importation under bond and drawback, and meet FAA airworthiness, registration, FCC and ITAR rules.

how to import an aircraft into the us

tariffEngineering.intro:
Almost every Chapter 88 line is Free under the general rate, so the levers are about the extra duties, and the biggest one is **civil-aircraft status**. An aircraft, engine, part or ground flight simulator that meets general note 6 (used in aircraft and covered by an FAA certificate or an FAA-recognized foreign airworthiness approval) is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties and Brazil's 25%. The importer claims it by entering the goods with special program indicator **"C"** where a "Free (C)" rate is printed, is deemed to certify civil use, and must keep the order or contract and airworthiness evidence (19 CFR 10.183). For Chapter 99 relief, notes 52(d) and 50(a)(iv) apply whether or not "Free (C)" is claimed, but the article must still meet general note 6.

Then: claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican goods; for drones, use the partner critical-components certification or an approved onshoring plan; use the Chapter 98 provisions for aircraft and parts repaired abroad, returned or brought in temporarily; and recover duties by drawback. Before an imported aircraft can fly it needs FAA airworthiness acceptance and U.S. registration; drones also need FCC authorization and, if military, ITAR rules apply. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim civil-aircraft status (general note 6)
levers.saves: 10% or 12.5% (2026 Section 301) and, for Brazil, 25%: certified civil aircraft and parts on the note 52(d) list pay none of them. Does not lift China's List 1 duty or the drone duty.
levers.appliesTo: 8801.00.00, 8802.11–8802.40, 8805.29, 8806, 8807.10, 8807.20, 8807.30, 8807.90.90 (not military aircraft, spacecraft, parachutes or satellite parts)
levers.document: Evidence that the article is used as original or replacement equipment in aircraft and is manufactured or operated under an FAA certificate or an FAA-recognized foreign airworthiness approval (or a pending or future application by a type and production certificate holder): the written order or contract plus the airworthiness documents, kept for CBP (19 CFR 10.183(e)). Enter with SPI "C" where "Free (C)" is printed; the importer is deemed to certify civil use.
levers.caveat: Articles purchased for the Department of Defense or the Coast Guard qualify only if they meet the use test and are FAA-certified or covered by an accepted application (19 CFR 10.183(b)). A claim may be made by amending the entry before liquidation is final, but refunds carry no interest (general note 6(a)).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 50(a)(iv) and 52(d)

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican aircraft and parts
levers.saves: 10% of value: the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canada (9903.05.29) or Mexico (9903.05.55), and the 3% base rate on parachutes
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada and Mexico, every heading
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in the importer's possession when the claim is made (19 CFR 182.12). Rules of origin: General Note 11.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not lift the Section 232 drone duty (note 43(b)). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Drones: certify allied critical components
levers.saves: Cuts the drone duty from 25% or 100% to 15% in all for products of the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and Liechtenstein (9903.08.24), or to +10% for the UK (9903.08.23)
levers.appliesTo: Drones of 8806.21–8806.99 and covered parts of 8807 from those countries
levers.document: The importer's certification that substantially all the critical components and technology are products of the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, an EU member or the UK, under the process Commerce establishes (Proclamation 11055 clause 4).
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duty is still added unless the drone meets general note 6.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 43(d)

levers.title: Drones: import under an approved onshoring plan
levers.saves: The whole Section 232 drone duty (25% or 100%), within the volumes the approval allows (9903.08.25 / 9903.08.26)
levers.appliesTo: Drones and covered parts (8806.21–8806.99, 8807) and production equipment for a company building U.S. drone production
levers.document: An onshoring plan approved by the Department of War, DHS or the Secretary of Commerce, committing to build, refurbish or expand a U.S. facility before January 20, 2029 (Proclamation 11055 clause 6).
levers.caveat: Benefits can be rescinded, retroactively in cases of fraud, if the company fails to meet its commitments.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 43

levers.title: Drones and parts: classify by weight, thermal imaging and end use
levers.saves: 75 points of drone duty (25% instead of 100%) for a drone up to 25 kg without thermal imaging; the whole drone duty for passenger drones (8806.10) and for 8807 parts used in manned aircraft or in drones up to 25 kg (9903.08.20)
levers.document: Specifications showing the maximum take-off weight (subheading note 2), whether a thermal imaging sensor is fitted, and, for parts, the aircraft or drone system they are for.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the article as imported. Flying toys designed solely for amusement are in 9503, not 8806 (chapter note 1). A binding ruling (19 CFR part 177) settles a doubtful case.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 43(c)

levers.title: Use the Chapter 98 provisions for repairs, returns and temporary entry
levers.saves: Duty on only the value of repairs or alterations made abroad (9802.00.40 / 9802.00.50), no duty on previously duty-paid aircraft engines and propellers re-imported unimproved (9801.00.30), and no duty at entry for aircraft and parts brought in temporarily for repair or processing and re-exported (9813.00.05, under bond)
levers.appliesTo: Aircraft, engines, propellers and parts sent abroad for maintenance, repair and overhaul, or brought in for U.S. MRO work
levers.document: For 9802: the foreign repairer's declaration and the importer's endorsement (19 CFR 10.8). For 9813: an entry under bond, re-export within the bond period (19 CFR 10.31).
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties apply to the value of repairs under 9802.00.40–.60 (notes 50(a) and 52(a)). Section 232 drone duties: goods claimed under Chapter 98 remain subject to the provision's terms (note 43(b)).

provisions.rate: Duty on the value of the repairs
provisions.text: Articles repaired or altered abroad under warranty

provisions.rate: Duty on the value of the repairs
provisions.text: Articles exported for repairs or alterations
Articles to be repaired, altered or processed in the United States and re-exported

levers.title: Recover duties by drawback when aircraft or parts are exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of duties paid on imported aircraft parts used to make, or re-exported as, exported goods
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable imports of any heading that are exported or used in exported aircraft
levers.document: A drawback claim under 19 CFR part 190 with import and export records.
levers.caveat: For the Section 232 drone duty only manufacturing drawback is allowed, and only for goods of trade-agreement partners with at least 85% partner content (Proclamation 11055 clause 8). Drones admitted to a foreign-trade zone must take privileged foreign status (clause 9).

rules.title: Civil-aircraft claims: entry with SPI "C" where printed, a deemed certification of civil use, and the order or contract plus airworthiness evidence kept for CBP (19 CFR 10.183(c)–(e), general note 6)

Imported aircraft need a U.S. type certificate issued on the basis of the exporting authority's certification under a bilateral agreement (14 CFR 21.29) and a standard airworthiness certificate (14 CFR 21.183(c)); foreign engines, propellers and articles are accepted only with an export airworthiness approval under such an agreement (14 CFR 21.500, 21.502)

Aircraft registration: an aircraft may be registered in the U.S. only if not registered abroad (14 CFR 47.3); one last registered in a foreign country needs evidence that the foreign registration has ended (14 CFR 47.37)

Drones: small unmanned aircraft must be registered before operation (14 CFR 48.15, 107.13), and drones produced for operation in U.S. airspace must meet the remote identification design and production rules (14 CFR part 89, subpart F)

Drones are radio-frequency devices: they may be imported only with a valid FCC equipment authorization or under a listed exception (47 CFR 2.1204), and drones and drone critical components produced abroad that are on the Covered List cannot get new authorizations (47 CFR 2.903)
Section 232 drone duty: declare 9903.08.20–9903.08.26 with the 8806 or 8807 line; partner and onshoring rates need Commerce's certification or approval (Proclamation 11055, U.S. note 43)

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 43

rules.title: Military aircraft and parts: U.S.-origin defense articles may be temporarily imported for servicing and re-exported without a license (22 CFR 123.4); other defense-article imports follow the ITAR
2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties: report the country heading (9903.05.20–9903.05.84, 9903.05.01) or the civil-aircraft exemption heading (9903.05.88, 9903.05.05) with the Chapter 88 line

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 50 and 52
CBP CSMS # 69326983 (Section 301 forced labor import duties)

groups.label: Balloons and dirigibles; gliders, hang gliders and other non-powered aircraft
groups.note: Balloons and gliders are aircraft: FAA certification and registration apply, and civil ones can use general note 6.

groups.label: Other aircraft (for example, helicopters, airplanes, except unmanned aircraft of heading 8806); spacecraft (including satellites) and suborbital and spacecraft launch vehicles
groups.note: The core of the chapter: civil aircraft need FAA acceptance and registration; military statistical lines cannot use general note 6; spacecraft (8802.60) are not on the civil-aircraft list.

groups.label: Parachutes (including dirigible parachutes and paragliders) and rotochutes; parts thereof and accessories thereto
groups.note: Parachutes pay 3% and are outside the civil-aircraft list; USMCA and other FTAs make them Free.

groups.label: Aircraft launching gear; deck-arrestor or similar gear; ground flying trainers; parts of the foregoing articles
groups.note: Only other ground flying trainers (8805.29, civil flight simulators) are on the civil-aircraft list; launching gear and air combat simulators are not.

groups.label: Unmanned aircraft
groups.note: The most regulated group: Section 232 drone duty, FCC authorization and Covered List, FAA registration and remote ID.

groups.label: Parts of goods of heading 8801, 8802 or 8806
groups.note: Parts: the civil-aircraft statistical lines (.15, .30) refer to general note 6; parts for drones over 25 kg pay the drone duty.

faqs.question: Are aircraft and aircraft parts exempt from U.S. tariffs?
searchedAs: are aircraft parts exempt from tariffs
are aircraft parts exempt from us tariffs
faqs.answer: Mostly yes, if they are civil aircraft. 66 of the 67 Chapter 88 lines are Free at base, and civil aircraft, engines, parts and ground flight simulators that meet general note 6 (used in aircraft and covered by an FAA certificate or an FAA-recognized foreign approval) are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties (U.S. note 52(d), 9903.05.88) and Brazil's 25% (9903.05.05). Not exempt: military aircraft and parts, spacecraft and satellite parts, parachutes, China's 25% List 1 duty, and the Section 232 drone duty.

faqs.question: What is the civil aircraft tariff exemption and how do I claim it?
faqs.answer: It comes from the WTO Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft, implemented in general note 6 (special program indicator "C"). A civil aircraft article is used as original or replacement equipment in aircraft and is made or operated under an FAA certificate or an FAA-recognized foreign airworthiness approval; articles bought for the Department of Defense or Coast Guard qualify only if certified. The importer claims "Free (C)" where printed, is deemed to certify civil use, and keeps the order or contract and airworthiness evidence (19 CFR 10.183). The Chapter 99 exemptions (9903.05.88, 9903.05.05) apply whether or not "Free (C)" is claimed.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on drones?
faqs.answer: Since September 3, 2026 drones of 8806.21–8806.99 pay a Section 232 duty (Proclamation 11055): +25% for drones up to 25 kg without thermal imaging (9903.08.22) and +100% for those with thermal imaging or over 25 kg (9903.08.21), on top of other duties. A Chinese drone without thermal imaging pays 62.5% (12.5% + 25% List 1 + 25%); with thermal imaging 137.5%. Products on the Blue UAS or FCC Conditional Approval lists on September 2, 2026 start paying on February 9, 2027. Allied-component drones from the EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan pay 15% for the drone duty and UK drones +10%.

faqs.question: How much tariff is on a DJI drone?
faqs.answer: A drone made in China and classified in 8806.21–8806.93 (up to 25 kg) pays 12.5% (2026 Section 301, 9903.05.31) + 25% (Section 301 List 1, 9903.88.01) + the Section 232 drone duty of 25% without thermal imaging or 100% with it: 62.5% or 137.5% of the customs value. Drones also need a valid FCC equipment authorization to be imported (47 CFR 2.1204), and the FCC Covered List bars new authorizations for drones produced abroad (47 CFR 2.903).

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for drones?
faqs.answer: Heading 8806 (unmanned aircraft), split by passenger drones (8806.10), remote-controlled-only drones (8806.21–8806.29) and other drones (8806.91–8806.99), and by maximum take-off weight: up to 250 g, 250 g–7 kg, 7–25 kg, 25–150 kg and over 150 kg. All are Free at base. Drone parts go in 8807 (8807.30 for other parts of airplanes, helicopters or unmanned aircraft). Toy drones designed solely for amusement are in 9503, not 8806 (chapter note 1).

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for aircraft parts?
searchedAs: harmonized tariff code for aircraft parts
hts code for civil aircraft parts
faqs.answer: Parts that are not more specifically classified elsewhere go in 8807: propellers and rotors (8807.10), undercarriages (8807.20), other parts of airplanes, helicopters or drones (8807.30), parts of communications satellites (8807.90.30) and other parts (8807.90.90). Each has statistical lines for civil-aircraft use (for the Department of Defense or Coast Guard, or other) and for other use. All are Free at base. Engines (8411, 8407), instruments (9014) and many other aircraft components are classified in their own chapters.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for helicopters and helicopter parts?
searchedAs: hs code for helicopter spare parts
hs code for civil helicopter parts
faqs.answer: Helicopters are 8802.11 (unladen weight up to 2,000 kg) and 8802.12 (over 2,000 kg), with statistical lines for military, new and used. Rotors and their parts are 8807.10 and other helicopter parts 8807.30. All are Free at base; civil helicopters and parts that meet general note 6 are also exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.

faqs.question: Are there U.S. tariffs on Canadian aircraft and aircraft parts?
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA or general note 6. Canadian goods pay the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.29) only without a USMCA claim, and certified civil aircraft and parts are exempt anyway (9903.05.88). Canada's Section 338 duties list no Chapter 88 line. Drones pay the Section 232 drone duty even with USMCA. The 2025 IEEPA duty (25%, then 35%) ended February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $9.10B of Chapter 88 goods to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on Airbus aircraft?
faqs.answer: Not on certified civil aircraft. EU products pay the 2026 Section 301 duty of 10% in place of the base rate (9903.05.39), but general-note-6 civil aircraft and parts are exempt (9903.05.88), so a new Airbus airliner from France or Germany enters Free. The Airbus-dispute duties (10% from October 2019, 15% from March 2020 on new large aircraft from France, Germany, Spain and the UK) have been suspended since 2021. The 15% IEEPA reciprocal rate exempted EU civil aircraft from September 1, 2025 and ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Brazilian aircraft such as Embraer?
faqs.answer: Not on certified civil aircraft. Brazil pays 25% (9903.05.01) plus the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.27), but civil aircraft, engines, parts and simulators that meet general note 6 are exempt from both (9903.05.05, 9903.05.88). Non-certified Brazilian Chapter 88 goods pay 37.5%. Brazil's 2025 IEEPA duty of 40% also excepted civil aircraft and ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on UK aerospace goods?
faqs.answer: Certified UK civil aircraft and parts enter Free: the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty on the UK (9903.05.81) does not apply to general-note-6 civil aircraft (9903.05.88). Under the 2025 Economic Prosperity Deal UK civil aircraft were exempt from the 10% reciprocal tariff from June 30, 2025, until all IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026. Other UK Chapter 88 goods pay 10%; UK drones also pay the drone duty (+10% with the allied-components certification).

faqs.question: Is there a Section 232 tariff on aircraft?
faqs.answer: No duty on manned aircraft. Commerce's Section 232 investigation of commercial aircraft, jet engines and parts (begun May 1, 2025) found a threat to national security, but Proclamation 11040 (July 9, 2026) imposed no tariff and directed negotiations, with an update due within 180 days. Section 232 does apply to drones (Proclamation 11055, from September 3, 2026).

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on aircraft parts from China?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on aircraft parts
faqs.answer: Chinese aircraft parts of 8807 pay 25% under Section 301 List 1 (9903.88.01) plus 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31): 37.5%. Certified civil aircraft parts are exempt only from the 12.5%, so they pay 25%. From most other suppliers certified civil aircraft parts are Free.

faqs.question: How do I import an aircraft into the United States?
searchedAs: importing an aircraft into the united states
how to import an aircraft into the us
faqs.answer: File a CBP entry under the 8802 line (Free at base) with the Chapter 99 heading for its origin, or the civil-aircraft exemption heading 9903.05.88 for a general-note-6 civil aircraft, keeping the airworthiness evidence (19 CFR 10.183). To fly it, the FAA must accept it: a type certificate based on the exporting authority's certification under a bilateral agreement (14 CFR 21.29) and a standard airworthiness certificate (14 CFR 21.183(c)). It must be registered in the U.S., with evidence that any foreign registration has ended (14 CFR 47.3, 47.37).

faqs.question: Where do U.S. aircraft imports come from?
faqs.answer: U.S. imports of Chapter 88 goods were $33.85B in 2025 (UN Comtrade, CIF). Canada ($9.10B) and France ($6.14B) supplied 45%, followed by Germany, the UK, Brazil, Japan and Mexico. Parts (8807, $17.55B) and complete aircraft (8802, $15.49B) make up almost all of it; drones were $190.5M.
